title: Early frostbite (frostnip / superficial frostbite)
summary: Fingers, toes, ears, nose, or cheeks that have gone white, waxy, or numb after cold exposure. Early frostbite can usually be rewarmed safely if there is no risk of refreezing.
steps: Get the person into a warm, sheltered place.
Treat any hypothermia first — see [[hypothermia-mild]]. A cold core makes frostbite rewarming dangerous.
Remove anything tight or wet near the frostbitten part — rings, watches, wet gloves, tight boots.
Rewarm the affected part in clean water that feels comfortably warm to a normal hand — not hot. Test the water yourself first; the frozen part cannot feel temperature.
Soak for 20–30 minutes until the skin turns pink or red and feels warm. It may sting or burn as it thaws — that is normal.
After rewarming, dry gently and wrap loosely in clean dry dressings. Place dry gauze or cloth between fingers and toes.
Keep the rewarmed part elevated, supported, and warm. Do not walk on a thawed foot.
avoid: Do not rub the frostbitten area with snow, hands, or cloth — ice crystals damage tissue further.
Do not rewarm with direct heat: fires, stoves, hot water bottles, hair dryers, heating pads. Burns are easy because feeling is lost.
Do not start rewarming if there is any chance the part might refreeze before reaching medical care. Refreezing causes much worse damage than staying frozen.
Do not burst blisters that form during thawing.
Do not give alcohol or cigarettes — both worsen circulation.
whenToEscalate: Always — every frostbite needs medical assessment, even if it looks like it has fully recovered.
Emergency if: skin stays black, blue, or hard after rewarming, large blisters develop, or the part remains numb after warming.
Combined hypothermia and frostbite — emergency. Treat the body core first.
Diabetic, vascular disease, or elderly people — extra urgent.
specialty: Emergency department; specialist burns or wound unit for deep frostbite.
